notes.17:7: Latin 'sacramentum' here renders Greek 'mysterion' (shifting from 'mysterium' in 17:5) in its biblical Latin sense of a sacred mystery or hidden meaning.
notes.17:8: The Clementine Vulgate reads 'quæ erat, et non est' ('which was and is not'), omitting the third clause 'and is to come' found in Greek manuscripts.
notes.17:12: The Vulgate reads 'post bestiam' ('after the beast') with the future tense 'accipient' ('will receive'), whereas the Greek text reads 'with the beast' in the present tense.
notes.17:16: The Vulgate reads 'in bestia' ('on the beast'), making only the ten horns the subject of the hatred, whereas critical Greek texts read 'and the beast' as a joint subject.
notes.17:17: The Vulgate reads 'quod placitum est illi' ('what is pleasing to Him') and omits the Greek clause 'and to act with one purpose' before 'to give their kingdom to the beast.'
notes.18:5: The Vulgate reads 'Dominus' ('the Lord') where Greek manuscripts read 'God,' and 'pervenerunt' ('have reached') where critical Greek texts read 'have been heaped up.'
notes.18:8: The Vulgate reads simply 'Deus' ('God') with the future tense 'judicabit' ('will judge'), whereas Greek manuscripts read 'the Lord God' with a past participle ('who has judged').
notes.18:12: The Vulgate reads 'de lapide pretioso' ('of precious stone'), whereas Greek manuscripts read 'of most costly wood.'
notes.18:17: The Vulgate reads 'in lacum navigat' ('sails on a lake'), a distinctive Latin reading contrasting with the Greek 'sails to a place' (i.e., voyagers or passengers).
notes.18:18: The Vulgate reads 'locum incendii ejus' ('the place of her burning'), contrasting with the Greek reading 'the smoke of her burning.'
notes.19:1: The Clementine Vulgate reads the plural "turbarum multarum" ("of many crowds"), whereas Greek manuscripts have the singular "a great crowd."
notes.19:2: The Vulgate uses the relative pronoun "qui" ("of Him who passed judgment") rather than the causal conjunction "because" found in the Greek, and has the plural "manibus" ("hands") rather than singular "hand."
notes.19:13: The Vulgate reads "aspersa sanguine" ("sprinkled with blood"), reflecting the Latin textual tradition rather than the Greek majority reading "dipped in blood."
notes.19:15: The Vulgate specifies "ex utraque parte acutus" ("sharp on both sides") where critical Greek texts have simply "sharp," and renders Greek "poimanei" ("shepherd") as "reget" ("will rule").
notes.19:16: The Vulgate omits the word "name" before "scriptum" ("written") and translates Greek "Lord of lords" with the participle "Dominus dominantium" ("Lord of those who rule").
notes.20:4: Latin "sedes" ("seats") is distinct from "thronus" ("throne," e.g., 20:11), forming a cognate pairing with "sederunt" ("sat").
notes.20:8: In Clementine Vulgate verse numbering, verse 8 combines what modern editions divide as verses 7 and 8, leaving no separate verse 7.
notes.20:10: The Clementine Vulgate places the fire clause in verse 10 rather than verse 9, includes "a Deo" ("from God"), and makes the beast and false prophet direct subjects of "cruciabuntur" ("will be tormented").
notes.20:14: Latin "infernus" denotes the underworld or realm of the dead (Greek "Hades"); the Vulgate reverses the order to "the underworld and death" and ends with "This is the second death" without adding "the lake of fire."
notes.21:2: The Vulgate includes "Et ego Joannes" ("And I, John"), a reading absent from most modern critical Greek editions.
notes.21:5: Latin "fidelissima" uses the superlative ("most faithful") where the Greek has the positive adjective ("trustworthy/faithful").
notes.21:7: Latin "possidebit" literally means "will possess" rather than "will inherit" (Greek "kleronomesei").
notes.21:11: Here and in 21:23 the Vulgate uses "claritas" ("radiance") rather than "gloria" ("glory," used in 21:24, 26), and renders the final comparison simply as "sicut crystallum" ("like crystal").
notes.21:16: The Vulgate specifies "aurea" ("golden") again for the reed and lists the equal dimensions in the order "length and height and width"; twelve thousand stadia is roughly 1,400 miles (2,200 kilometers).
notes.22:3: The Clementine Vulgate uses the plural verb erunt with sedes ("the thrones of God and of the Lamb will be in it"), whereas the Greek has the singular ("the throne ... will be"), though the following pronouns ejus and illi ("His ... Him") remain singular.
notes.22:11: The Vulgate reads the passive justificetur ("be justified still"), reflecting a Greek variant, whereas most modern critical Greek texts read "still do righteousness."
notes.22:14: The Clementine Vulgate includes in sanguine Agni ("in the blood of the Lamb"), echoing Revelation 7:14, whereas Greek manuscripts either omit this phrase or read "do His commandments."
notes.22:19: The Vulgate reads de libro vitæ ("from the book of life") and includes et de his ("and from the things"), whereas the critical Greek text reads "from the tree of life" without the following "and from."
notes.22:20: Following the Clementine punctuation (a colon at the end of v. 19 and a period after istorum), dicit qui testimonium perhibet istorum concludes the warning of vv. 18-19, whereas Greek editions link this clause forward to introduce "Yes, I am coming soon."
